splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability under ERISA must be locked in by the end of the prior plan year or can be selected afterward. The outcome affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be selected no later than the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing the use of more current data in calculating withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects how federal courts calculate sentencing at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the supervised release term is tolled during the period the supervisee absconds, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the originally specified term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and the term expires as originally set regardless of absconding.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) — which prohibits raising any claim previously presented — when bringing successive collateral attacks under § 2255. If it applies, federal prisoners are barred from re-raising any prior claim in addition to satisfying § 2255(h)'s separate requirements.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that federal prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements (newly discovered evidence or new constitutional rule) and are not subject to the additional categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The outcome could reshape how courts evaluate whether candidates can challenge election rules before an election takes place, potentially affecting rules on mail-in voting and ballot counting deadlines nationwide.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates for federal office have Article III standing to challenge election administration rules that may affect the outcome of their election, including ballot-receipt deadlines.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have Article III standing to challenge state election administration laws pre-election because they cannot show a sufficiently concrete and particularized injury.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over Auer/Kisor deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations when construing ambiguous provisions that carry criminal consequences.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should apply agency deference (Auer/Kisor) or the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous Sentencing Guidelines or criminal regulatory provisions. At least three circuits hold lenity trumps deference, while the Third Circuit has held that deference trumps lenity. The issue has heightened significance after Loper Bright overruled Chevron.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity should prevail over agency or Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous provisions with criminal consequences, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through interpretive guidance.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that Auer/Kisor deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary controls even in criminal sentencing contexts, overriding the rule of lenity when the Commission has offered an authoritative interpretation.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' means 'and' or 'or' in the safety-valve provision of the First Step Act. The Ninth and Eleventh Circuits hold that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria, while the Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Circuits hold that possessing any one criterion is disqualifying. This creates disparate sentencing outcomes across the country.

positions.label: Conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' is conjunctive, so defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they satisfy all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1).

positions.label: Disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' operates disjunctively (or distributively), so that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which includes inchoate offenses (conspiracy, attempt, aiding and abetting) in the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid and authoritative interpretation of the career-offender guideline.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary adding inchoate offenses to the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in the career-offender guideline is entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor or impermissibly expands the guideline's text. This directly affects whether conspiracy or attempt convictions trigger the career-offender enhancement, significantly impacting sentences.

positions.label: Commentary is valid and entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1's inclusion of inchoate offenses is a permissible interpretation of the ambiguous guideline text and is entitled to controlling weight under Stinson and Kisor.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands the guideline
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that Application Note 1 cannot be given deference because it adds to rather than interprets the guideline.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the substance is controlled under state law but not under the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be federally scheduled. Some circuits hold the Guidelines' reference to state law offenses includes substances controlled only under state law, while others require a match with the federal schedules.

positions.label: No federal-schedule match required
positions.summary: Holds that U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) broadly defines 'controlled substance offense' to include state law offenses regardless of whether the substance is also federally controlled, finding no textual basis to graft a federal law limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Federal-schedule match required
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines only if the substance at issue is also controlled under federal law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in law can contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. The Eighth Circuit categorically bars reliance on such changes, while other circuits have allowed consideration of non-retroactive sentencing changes, especially after the Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6). The Seventh Circuit has held the Commission exceeded its authority in promulgating that policy statement.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and the Sentencing Commission's contrary policy statement exceeds its statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law can be considered as part of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, particularly under the Sentencing Commission's amended policy statement at U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits split on whether appreciation in property value between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that such appreciation belongs to the estate, while other circuits have reached the opposite conclusion, creating a conflict on the scope of 'property of the estate' upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion increases in equity belong to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7, based on the broad scope of § 541(a).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the debtors, not the estate, consistent with the structure, policies, and legislative history of § 348(f).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release at revocation proceedings, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to the purposes of supervised release (deterrence, public protection, rehabilitation).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the permissible purposes of sentences imposed upon revocation of supervised release. The Sixth Circuit allows district courts to expressly punish defendants for supervised release violations, while other circuits hold that revocation sentences should serve only forward-looking purposes such as deterrence and public safety, not retribution for the violation itself.

positions.label: Courts may punish for the violation
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may impose revocation sentences that expressly punish defendants for their violations of supervised release conditions.

positions.label: Courts may not punish for the violation
positions.summary: Holds that sentences upon revocation of supervised release should serve the limited purposes of deterrence, public protection, and rehabilitation, not retribution for the violation.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must bring challenges to the conditions or terms of their confinement exclusively through habeas corpus, or whether such claims may also be brought as civil rights actions (e.g., Bivens).
splits.description: Circuits have long disagreed on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy for challenges to conditions of confinement that do not directly challenge the fact or duration of imprisonment, or whether civil rights actions are also available. This unresolved conflict affects how prisoners challenge BOP decisions regarding earned time credits, transfers to prerelease custody, and other non-release conditions.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy
positions.summary: Holds that challenges affecting the execution of a sentence, including conditions and terms of confinement, must be brought through habeas corpus and cannot proceed as civil rights actions.

positions.label: Civil rights actions are also available
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions of confinement that do not directly challenge the fact or duration of imprisonment may proceed as civil rights actions and are not limited to habeas corpus.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to an order denying attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment in a criminal case.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (subject to the 30-day civil appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case (subject to the 14-day criminal appeal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view applying the civil deadline, noting a lopsided circuit split on this issue.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, and thus the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fee motion is part of the criminal case, so the shorter 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal medical records in litigation is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: Circuits are not fully aligned on whether denials of motions to seal documents containing sensitive medical information qualify for immediate appeal under the collateral order doctrine. The D.C. Circuit held that maintaining medical privacy is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate review, noting the strength of the interest recognized by other circuits, though the extent of disagreement across circuits varies.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that an order denying a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of high order that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying sealing motions generally are not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine, as the interest can be adequately vindicated through other means including post-judgment appeal.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to review the Second Circuit's approach to legal questions governing how business operators must treat customers and what remedies are available for disputes, suggesting a circuit split on standards for fair treatment, discrimination liability, and damages in service industries.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applied a particular standard for evaluating discrimination or unfair treatment claims in hospitality settings that the Supreme Court found sufficiently important or unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Other circuits' approach
positions.summary: Other circuits have applied different standards for evaluating such claims, creating a split that prompted Supreme Court review.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
